The Atlas concedes that permanent bans are practically unenf

title: The Atlas admits its ultimate sanction cannot actually be permanent, and proposes reputation as the real barrier
content:
NR-9 states the problem with unusual bluntness. A.1.5.10 defines derecognition as "permanently removing" an entity from the AC role, and NR-9 replies: "In fact, it is not possible to effect such a permanent removal. Given the presence of anonymous/pseudonymous actors in the decentralized 'workforce' of the Sky ecosystem, a known identity of an actor can be barred from an AC role; and yet that actor can easily re-enter the system under a different pseudonym or identity."

This is a direct consequence of two other commitments colliding. A.1.5.7 *requires* AD and Facilitator anonymity, and A.1.5.10 relies on identity-based exclusion. A framework cannot both mandate that role holders be unidentifiable and enforce a lifetime ban on identified persons — the register at A.1.5.10.2 can only list "identity and known aliases," which is precisely the information a returning actor discards.

The proposed mitigation reframes the barrier from identity to accumulated standing: "A robust reputation system is already planned; by tracking reputation that is earned over a long timescale, a derecognized entity would be barred from quickly regaining a foothold." The operative word is *quickly*. This is not exclusion but a re-entry cost — a fresh pseudonym starts with no history, and if roles of consequence require long-earned reputation, the practical effect approximates a ban without depending on identification.

The honest reading is that the ultimate sanction is weaker than its text claims, and that the AC regime's severity elsewhere — mandatory derecognition, 51% thresholds, inverted burdens — partly reflects this. If removal is only temporary in effect, removing readily is cheaper than removing carefully. It also gives a specific reason why the derecognition notice's contents matter so much: A.1.5.5.0.4.1.1.2.var1 suggests including discovered evidence in the notice precisely because it "can impact the reputation score of Entity."
description: NR-9 concedes a derecognized pseudonymous actor 'can easily re-enter the system under a different pseudonym', so exclusion depends on long-timescale reputation rather than identity bans.
